title: Les lettres muettes
intro: French spelling has many letters you don't pronounce. A few simple rules tell you which ones — and when a silent letter suddenly wakes up. Press 🔊 on every example and repeat it out loud.

cases.label: final consonants: silent
cases.rule: Most consonants at the end of a word are silent: *petit, grand, vous, trois, Paris*.

cases.label: C, R, F, L: often heard
cases.rule: Final **c, r, f, l** are often pronounced (think *CaReFuL*): *avec, bonjour, neuf, il*. But **-er** verbs end in /e/: *aimer*.

cases.label: final -e: silent, but…
cases.rule: A final **-e** is silent, but it makes the consonant before it heard: *petit* /pə.ti/ → *petite* /pə.tit/.

cases.label: plural -s: silent
cases.rule: The plural **-s** is silent: *frère* and *frères* sound the same. Listen to the article instead: *le* /lə/ → *les* /le/.

cases.label: verb ending -ent: silent
cases.rule: **-ent** at the end of a verb is silent: *ils parlent* sounds like *il parle*.

cases.label: h: always silent
cases.rule: The **h** is never pronounced. Most words with h act as if they start with a vowel: *l'homme, j'habite, les‿hommes*.

cases.label: liaison: a silent letter wakes up
cases.rule: Before a vowel, a silent final letter can link to the next word: **s / x → /z/** (*les‿enfants*), **n** (*un‿ami*), **t** (*vingt‿ans*).

cases.label: six, huit, dix: three sounds
cases.rule: Alone: /sis/, /ɥit/, /dis/. Before a consonant: /si/, /ɥi/, /di/. Before a vowel: /siz/, /ɥit/, /diz/.

sections.title: 1. Final consonants are usually silent
sections.tip: When a word ends in a consonant, guess **silent** first — you'll be right most of the time.

sections.title: 2. …but C, R, F, L are often heard
text: Remember the English word **CaReFuL**: final **c, r, f, l** are often pronounced.
sections.tip: Big exception: verbs ending in **-er** end in the sound /e/: *aimer, habiter, parler*.

sections.title: 3. Final -e: silent, but it wakes up the consonant
text: This is how you hear the difference between masculine and feminine.

examples.fr: Mon frère est {petit|snd-e}, ma sœur est {petite|snd-e}.
examples.en: My brother is small, my sister is small.

sections.tip: If the masculine already ends in a vowel, both sound the same: *marié / mariée*.

sections.title: 5. The letter h is always silent
text: French **h** makes no sound. With most words it behaves like a vowel: *l'homme, j'habite, les‿hommes* /le.zɔm/.
sections.tip: A few words have an “aspirated h” that blocks this (*le haricot*, the bean). You'll meet them later.

sections.title: 6. Liaison: a silent letter wakes up
text: Inside a group of words that belong together (article + noun, pronoun + verb, number + noun), a silent final letter links to a following vowel. **s** and **x** sound /z/, **t** and **d** sound /t/.

sections.title: 7. Numbers: six, huit, dix have three sounds

mistakes.why: The final **t** is silent. You only hear it in the feminine: *petite*.

story.title: La famille Dupont
story.en: A short text to read aloud. Listen first, then read along with the speaker.

lines.en: Mr and Mrs Dupont live in Paris.

lines.fr: {Les enfants|snd-liaison} ont {dix ans|snd-numbers}, {huit ans|snd-numbers}, {six ans|snd-numbers}, {cinq ans|snd-numbers}, {trois ans|snd-liaison} et {un an|snd-liaison}.
lines.en: The children are ten, eight, six, five, three and one.

lines.fr: Le {grand|snd-final} frère s'appelle Paul. Sa sœur, Claire, est {grande|snd-e} aussi.
lines.en: The big brother is called Paul. His sister Claire is tall too.
The little ones play with their grandfather.

lines.fr: Grand-père a {quatre-vingts ans|snd-liaison} et il {habite|snd-h} {avec|snd-careful} eux.
lines.en: Grandpa is eighty and he lives with them.

lines.fr: Le soir, toute la famille dit : « {Bonsoir|snd-careful} ! »
lines.en: In the evening, the whole family says: “Good evening!”

lines.fr: Et la maison des {Dupont|snd-final} ? C'est une très {grande|snd-e} maison !
lines.en: And the Duponts' house? It's a very big house!
